content: A malaria vaccine is urgently needed to combat the disease. SPf66 was one of the earliest malaria vaccines developed. It is a synthetic peptide vaccine that combines antigens from the blood stages of malaria with an antigen from the sporozoite stage. The vaccine primarily targets the blood (asexual) stages of the malaria parasite. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of the SPf66 vaccine in preventing infection, disease, and death caused by Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, and P. ovale. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and the Science Citation Index, covering studies up to March 2008. Additionally, reference lists of articles were reviewed, and researchers and organizations in the field were contacted. The study included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared the SPf66 vaccine with either a placebo or standard antimalarial control measures. Participants of any age who were exposed to malaria either through artificial challenge or natural exposure were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data, including information on adverse events. The results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of ten efficacy trials involving 9,698 participants were analyzed. The results regarding the effectiveness of SPf66 in reducing new episodes of P. falciparum malaria were inconsistent. In four trials conducted in Africa, the vaccine showed no significant effect (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.07; 2,371 participants). Similarly, in one trial conducted in Asia, the vaccine was not effective (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.25; 1,221 participants). However, in four trials conducted in South America, the vaccine reduced the number of first attacks of P. falciparum malaria by 28% (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.82; 3,807 participants). The vaccine did not demonstrate any reduction in episodes of P. vivax malaria or in hospital admissions due to severe malaria. Importantly, no serious adverse events were reported in association with the SPf66 vaccine. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support the use of the SPf66 vaccine for protection against P. falciparum malaria in Africa. While there was a modest reduction in P. falciparum malaria attacks in South America, the current formulation of SPf66 does not justify further trials. However, further research may be warranted to explore new formulations of the SPf66 vaccine or its use in South America.
